paras: The Vineland manhunt was a three-day pursuit in August 1920 by posses of white residents of Jefferson County, Missouri, after a Black man accused of attempting to attack a white girl, Gertrude Wilson, near Vineland on August 11. The man, who gave his name as David Robinson of Chicago, was shot and wounded, captured near Blackwell on August 14, and jailed at Hillsboro rather than lynched. Wire services carried the hunt nationally, one headline announcing a search 'to lynch him'.

Wilson's age was given as 12 by the wire services, 14 by two regional papers and 18 by the Black Dispatch. According to the United Press, a man stopped her horse as she rode to the post office, and when she screamed, people from a nearby farmhouse came and he fled. An International News Service dispatch said instead that he carried her into the bushes.

A posse searched through the night; it numbered 300 by August 12 and later reached 400. That morning a man named Politte fired on the fugitive at his farm and wounded him, though reports named him variously as T. M. Pollitte, P. M. Polittee and a son of Tom Politte. The INS reported that 'threats of a lynching were made', while the United Press quoted posse members denying he would be lynched.

The chase covered nearly 100 miles through three counties and ended near its starting point. On the morning of August 14, Clyde Nicholson, a young visitor from Richwoods, met the fugitive alone, fired six revolver shots at him, and took his surrender. He had been wounded twice earlier, and a physician called the injuries not serious.

His captors said they would turn him over to the Jefferson County authorities, and Sheriff Frank Clark came to arrest him. The INS reported that a lynching was feared if the girl identified him. The East St. Louis Daily Journal said he had confessed and was brought to De Soto under special guard with no attempt at mob rule. The Potosi Journal reported 'some talk of a necktie party' but said 'wiser counsel prevailed' and he was jailed at Hillsboro.

Tom Politte, a 65-year-old farmer in the chase, dropped dead on hearing of the capture. A De Soto bank cashier, O. H. White, announced the sale of photographs of the prisoner and his captor to pay $170 for the bloodhounds. In September the Potosi Journal reported that the Jefferson County court had found Robinson insane and sent him to the state asylum at Fulton. No report of a trial on the assault charge appears in the coverage.

The INS story ran in the Lake County Times of Hammond, Indiana, under 'SEEK NEGRO TO LYNCH HIM', and on August 13 the Evening Missourian headlined 'POSSE KILLS NEGRO', a report the United Press called erroneous the next day. United Press capture briefs ran on August 14 from Oregon to South Dakota, most calling him an 'unidentified negro' and saying a lynching was feared. Headlines such as 'Negro Assaulter Is Captured' treated the accusation as fact, and the Chattanooga News titled its story 'Angry Mob Finds Negro in Swamp'. The story ran in the Lake County Times and Rock Island Argus that day and as late as August 19 in the Kenosha Telegraph-Courier, under a 'Vinland, Md.' dateline.
Nearby papers added local detail: the East St. Louis Daily Journal on the failure of East St. Louis bloodhounds and the calm at De Soto, the Potosi Journal on the 'necktie party' talk.

The only Black-press account found, a De Soto correspondence in the Black Dispatch of August 27, ran as 'CHASE ENDS; NO LYNCHING'. Where white papers wrote of posses and farmers, it described 'a mob of whites' that chased him nearly a hundred miles and shot at him many times. It reported that he admitted the charge before the girl and that she and her father said to let the law take its course.

Accounts gave his name as Davis Robinson, David Robinson and David Robertson. His wounds were placed in the head, back and legs, the head, back and arm, or the chest and leg. Only the East St. Louis Daily Journal and the Black Dispatch report a confession.

accounts.label: United Press wire
accounts.gist: A man stopped the girl's horse; she screamed and neighbors drove him off. Three hundred residents hunted him; the posse denied it would lynch him, though one version promised 'speedy punishment'.

accounts.label: International News Service wire
accounts.gist: The man carried the girl into the bushes; angry farmers tracked him by his blood and made lynching threats; after capture a lynching was feared if she identified him.

accounts.label: East St. Louis Daily Journal (De Soto dispatch)
accounts.gist: The prisoner was said to have confessed; he was brought to De Soto under special guard and no mob attempt was made.

accounts.label: Potosi Journal (neighboring county weekly)
accounts.gist: Nicholson's shots missed; there was talk of a 'necktie party' but the prisoner was jailed at Hillsboro; a month later he was found insane.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Black Dispatch)
accounts.gist: A 'mob of whites' chased him nearly a hundred miles and shot at him many times; before the girl he admitted the charge, and she and her father told the crowd to let the law take its course.

framing.detail: INS headline 'SEEK NEGRO TO LYNCH HIM' and 'ANGRY MOB FINDS NEGRO IN SWAMP' presented the lynching threat openly while calling the accusation a charge.
UP briefs called him the 'assailant' or 'Negro Assaulter', described the crime as fact, and said a lynching was feared.
The Potosi Journal called it the 'Vineland Man Hunt', spoke of 'his attempted crime' as fact, and treated lynching talk as a 'necktie party' that 'wiser counsel' averted.
The East St. Louis Daily Journal stressed the failed local bloodhounds, the absence of mob action at De Soto, and the photograph sale.
The Black Dispatch headline 'CHASE ENDS; NO LYNCHING' and the phrase 'a mob of whites' cast the pursuers as a mob rather than a posse, while reporting the charge and his admission without comment.
